assessment.nobel_worthiness: A consequential body of work that made the long-run evolution and institutional determinants of income and wealth inequality measurable and central to economic analysis.
assessment.attribution: Piketty, Saez and Zucman form a coherent core linking historical distributional series, top-income measurement and offshore-wealth evidence.
assessment.maturity: The research programme has generated extensive empirical use and sustained debate across public finance, macroeconomics and economic history.
uncertainties: Some estimates and interpretations remain contested, especially across countries and wealth components.
The appropriate division of credit among the wider inequality-measurement literature is difficult.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work transformed understanding of how technology, trade exposure and task change reshape local labour markets and wage inequality.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson provide a particularly identifiable empirical and conceptual collaboration on trade shocks, tasks and distributional consequences.
assessment.maturity: Its findings and research designs have been influential for more than a decade and have shaped a broad subsequent literature.
uncertainties: The size and persistence of local adjustment effects depend on setting and specification.
Technology and trade are difficult to separate fully in observed labour-market change.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population administrative data were used to give intergenerational mobility an unusually concrete geographic, institutional and policy-relevant empirical foundation.
assessment.attribution: Chetty, Hendren and Friedman are central to the linked mobility-data programme and its influential measurement architecture.
assessment.maturity: The programme is well established, replicated in extensions and widely used in research and policy discussion.
uncertainties: Associations between childhood place and later outcomes do not by themselves identify every causal mechanism.
Credit allocation also involves important contributions by other collaborators and earlier mobility researchers.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework gave growth and development research a powerful, empirically operational account of how distorted input allocation can lower aggregate productivity.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh, Klenow and Restuccia are the natural core for the closely connected contribution described.
assessment.maturity: The framework has become a standard reference point in macro-development and firm-level productivity research.
uncertainties: Measured dispersion can reflect technology, adjustment frictions or data limitations as well as distortions.
Quantitative welfare and income implications are model-dependent.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work supplied enduring economic foundations for valuing exhaustible resources, biodiversity and wealth inclusive of natural capital.
assessment.attribution: Dasgupta and Heal are closely associated with the fundamental dynamic treatment of resource scarcity and its welfare implications.
assessment.maturity: The contribution is longstanding and increasingly relevant to environmental accounting and sustainability policy.
uncertainties: The measurement and valuation of biodiversity and natural capital remain intrinsically difficult.
Later work across environmental economics complicates any narrow attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The research clarified how agglomeration, cities, housing and local productivity jointly shape the spatial distribution of economic activity.
assessment.attribution: Glaeser, Puga and Moretti represent a strong core spanning urban evidence, agglomeration mechanisms and modern local-labour-market consequences.
assessment.maturity: The field has accumulated substantial theoretical and empirical evidence, with clear relevance for regional development.
uncertainties: The proposed discovery combines several partly distinct literatures.
Housing supply, amenities and sorting make causal attribution in city outcomes challenging.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evolutionary analysis of routines and organisational capabilities offered a durable alternative account of firm behaviour, innovation and economic dynamism.
assessment.attribution: Winter is unmistakably central to the contribution, though the intellectual programme is associated with a broader scholarly tradition.
assessment.maturity: The ideas have had long-standing influence in organisational economics, innovation studies and management research.
uncertainties: The empirical operationalisation of routines and evolutionary mechanisms is less unified than the conceptual contribution.
Attribution is complicated by foundational collaborators outside the listed candidate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Research on early-life conditions and skill formation established that health and developmental environments can have persistent economic consequences.
assessment.attribution: Currie, Almond and Cunha provide complementary empirical and theoretical contributions to the stated programme.
assessment.maturity: The area has produced a substantial body of evidence and strongly influenced education, health and labour economics.
uncertainties: Identification of long-run causal pathways remains sensitive to context and empirical design.
The contribution overlaps with a large interdisciplinary human-capital literature.
